=== projectDescription ===
NRAS activating mutations occur in 15-25% of melanoma patients. However, this subtype is more aggressive and refractory to current treatment modalities, including targeted MEK inhibitors, immunotherapies, and the recently emerging RAS inhibitors. Accordingly, identifying novel therapeutic targets and designing novel antimelanoma strategies is of utmost clinical relevance. Melanomas often harbor hyperactive nitric oxide synthases (NOS) which correlates strongly with poor prognosis. NOS is also known to be activated by ERK signaling. The nitric oxide so produced, induces nitrosylation, a post-translational modification, which dysregulates various kinases and phosphatases. We sensitized NRAS-mutant melanomas to targeted MEK inhibitors by inhibiting nitrosylation. This outcome revealed a strong correlation between global de-nitrosylation and downregulation of MEK-ERK cascade with a concomitant de-nitrosylation of NRAS and other small GTPases like Rho and Rac, dual specificity phosphatases, and ribosomal S6 kinase. In vivo, we observed extreme regression of NRAS-mutant melanoma tumors generated in an immunocompetent mouse model in response to a sequential nitrosylation inhibition and MEK inhibition. In addition to MEK-ERK downregulation, this strategy activated the CD8+ T cells in the tumor microenvironment. We conclude that while nitrosylation hyperactivates the RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK cascade, it also suppresses anti-melanoma immune response, bolstering progression and MEKi resistance. The underlying mechanism(s) will be crucial in identifying novel therapeutic vulnerabilities against aggressive, currently incurable NRAS-mutant melanomas with potential clinical application in other melanoma subtypes.
=== sampleProcessingProtocol ===
The nitrosylated proteins were detected using the previously established Biotin Switch Technique with minor modifications. Cells were lysed in HENS buffer (Cat. No. 90106, ThermoFisher Scientific), supplemented with a protease cocktail inhibitor (Cat. 78429, ThermoFisher Scientific). For efficient blocking of free thiols, the pH of HENS should be 6-6.5. The protein concentrations were estimated by BCA protein estimation kit (Cat. No. 23225, ThermoFisher Scientific). Free thiols (-SH groups) were chemically blocked with 20 mM N-ethylmaleimide (NEM) (Cat. No. E1271, Millipore-Sigma) for 30 minutes at 50 °C, and excess NEM was removed by acetone precipitation(Cat. No. 67-64-1, Sigma). After resuspending the pellet in HENS, the S-nitrosylated (-SNO) thiols on Cysteines were reduced to -SH group using 1 mM ascorbate (Cat. No. PHR1279, Sigma), and labelled with biotin using 0.8 mM Biotin-HPDP (Cat. No. 16459, Cayman Chemicals) by incubation at room temperature for 2 hours in the dark. Excess labeling reagents were removed by Acetone precipitation. The protein pellets were washed twice with aqueous 70% acetone, dried for ~5 minutes at room temperature, and resuspended in HENS buffer. For electrophoretic analyses, 10-15 ug total biotin labelled lysate was used on pre-cast 4-20% SDS PAGE (Cat. 4561091, Bio-Rad, CA, USA). After transferring to the PVDF membranes (Cat. No. 162-0184) using standard procedures. As a positive control, nitrosylation was induced using chemical sources of nitric oxide; S-nitroso-L-glutathione or GSNO, formal name L-γ-glutamyl-S-nitroso-L-cysteinyl-glycine (Cat. 82240), and Diethylenetriamine or DETA-NONOate (Cat. 82120), both from Cayman Chemicals.   For identification of nitrosylated proteins, 400 - 800 µg of biotin-HPDP labeled protein was diluted with two volumes of neutralization buffer (20 mM HEPES, 100 mM NaCl, 1 mM EDTA, 0.5% v/v Triton X-100). Streptavidin magnetic beads (Cat. No. Z548C, Promega, WI, USA), or Streptavidin agarose resin (Cat. No. 20359, ThermoFisher Scientific) (30 µl bead slurry per 1 mg protein) were washed three times with 500 µl of neutralization buffer and added to the biotin-HPDP labeled protein. Incubation was carried out overnight at 4 0C. Beads were washed with neutralization buffer supplemented with 600 mM NaCl, followed by protein elution with elution buffers (Neutralization buffer + 5% β-mercaptoethanol), boiled on a heat block for 5-10 minutes. For mass spectrometry-based identification of the nitrosylated proteome (nitrosylome), the YUDOSO, YUTICA, and YUGASP cells were treated with 100 µM GSNO for 4-6 hours followed by BST to label the nitrosylated cysteines with biotin. Biotinylated proteins were recovered using neutravidin beads (Pierce), followed by trypsin digestion and peptide desalting. Cleaned peptides were labeled with TMT10plex reagents with the following channel layout: 3 YUDOSO-Control samples were labeled with 126C/127C/128C. 3 YUDOSO-GSNO samples were labeled with 127N/128N/129N. Inhibition sample was labeled with 130C and a negative control sample with 131N. After label incorporation check (LC-MS/MS and spectral counting of TMT-labeled versus underivatized peptides), all samples were combined and another neutravidin enrichment was performed to recover biotinylated peptides. The flowthrough peptides were separated with high-pH reversed phase offline fractionation cartridges into 4 fractions for protein identification. A nanoflow ultra high performance liquid chromatograph interfaced with an electrospray bench top orbitrap mass spectrometer (RSLCnano and Q Exactive HF-X, Thermo, San Jose, CA) was used for liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry peptide sequencing experiments.  The sample was first loaded onto a pre-column (C18 PepMap100, 100 µm ID x 2 cm length packed with 5 µm particle size, 100 Å pore size) and washed for 8 minutes with aqueous 2% acetonitrile with 0.1% formic acid.  The trapped peptides were eluted onto the analytical column, (C18 PepMap100, 75 µm ID x 25 cm length packed with 2 µm particles, 100 Å pore size, Thermo, San Jose, CA).  The 120-minute gradient was programmed as: 95% solvent A (2% acetonitrile + 0.1% formic acid) for 8 minutes, solvent B (aqueous 90% acetonitrile + 0.1% formic acid) from 5% to 38.5% in 90 minutes, then solvent B from 50% to 90% B in 7 minutes and held at 90% for 5 minutes, followed by solvent B from 90% to 5% in 1 minute and re-equilibration for 10 minutes.  The flow rate was 300 nl/min. Twenty tandem mass spectra were collected in a data-dependent manner following each survey scan. Spray voltage was 1900 V. Capillary temperature was 275°C. S-lens RF was set to 50. Normalized collision energy (NCE) was set at 27. The resolution settings were 60,000 and 45,000 for MS and MS/MS, respectively. The isolation window was 0.8 Th with 0.2 offset to capture the first two isotopes of each peptide for MS/MS.  Dynamic exclusion was set at 15 seconds.
=== dataProcessingProtocol ===
MaxQuant  (version 1.6.14.0) was used to identify proteins and quantify the TMT reporter ion intensities with default settings: Up to 2 missed trypsin cleavages were allowed. Carbamidomethyl cysteine was set as fixed modification. Biotin-HPDP and Methionine oxidation were set as variable modifications. Both Peptide Spectral Match and Protein FDR were set at 0.05. The human protein database was downloaded in March 2021 from Uniprot.org. Similar searches were performed in Mascot for this upload.

=== TITLE ===
Blocking Nitrosylation Induces Immunogenic Cell Death by Sensitizing NRAS-Mutant Melanoma to MEK Inhibitors
=== ABSTRACT ===
Nitrosylation-regulated molecular mechanisms present a vulnerability that can be exploited to sensitize NRAS-mutant melanomas to existing targeted therapies while enhancing antitumor immunity.

Abstract

Activating NRAS mutations occur in 15% to 25% of all melanomas. However, this subtype remains refractory to existing therapeutics, including immunotherapy and RAS inhibitors; therefore, identifying innovative treatment strategies is of utmost importance. We investigated the role of nitrosylation, a nitric oxide–induced posttranslational modification, in melanoma progression and therapeutic resistance. Inhibiting nitrosylation sensitized NRAS-mutant melanomas to targeted MEK inhibitors (MEKi), leading to sustained downregulation of the ERK-MAPK pathway, along with concomitant denitrosylation of NRAS, MEK, ERK, RSK1, and DUSPs. Global nitrosylome profiling using mass spectrometry revealed nitrosylation of multiple ERK regulators. Gain- and loss-of-function studies confirmed a positive association between nitrosylation and ERK activation. ERK and MEK proteins harbored potential nitrosylation sites, mutation of which abrogated their phosphorylation and inhibited cell growth. The nitrosylome also contained damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMP), factors known to induce immunogenic cell death (ICD). Notably, nitrosylation inhibition combined with MEKi markedly inhibited NRAS-mutant melanoma growth in an immunocompetent mouse model. This was accompanied by downregulated MEK-ERK signaling and extracellular release of DAMPs such as calreticulin, phospho-eIF2α, and HMGB1, confirming ICD induction. Furthermore, the combination significantly increased the repertoire of CD8+ T cells, dendritic cells, and macrophages in the tumor microenvironment, which was validated in cocultures of dendritic cells and T lymphocytes. In conclusion, the current study demonstrates that nitrosylation inhibition sensitizes NRAS-mutant melanomas to targeted MEKi-induced cell death and causes the release of non-nitrosylated (active) DAMPs that induce a potent antimelanoma immune response via ICD. These findings highlight potential therapeutic vulnerabilities in the currently untreatable NRAS-mutant melanoma subtype.

Significance:

Nitrosylation-regulated molecular mechanisms present a vulnerability that can be exploited to sensitize NRAS-mutant melanomas to existing targeted therapies while enhancing antitumor immunity.

Graphical Abstract
=== INTRO ===
Introduction

 NRAS-mutant melanoma is highly aggressive with a poor prognosis compared with other mutations. Despite panRAS and NRAS inhibitors being in preclinical/clinical stages, MEK inhibitors (MEKi), immunotherapy, or their combination show limited efficacy. Additionally, MEK inhibition combined with cell-cycle inhibitors or RAS-activated PI3K/AKT blockers has been ineffective, highlighting the need for novel therapeutic strategies.

Constitutive MEK-ERK activation in NRAS-/BRAF-mutant melanomas upregulates nitric oxide synthase (NOS; refs.), correlating with poor prognosis, making NOS a potential target. However, systemic NOS inhibition is impractical due to its physiologic role. Nitric oxide induces nitrosylation, a posttranslational modification (PTM) in which nitrogen monoxide attaches to cysteine, forming a nitrosyl group (-SNO), modulating kinase and phosphatase functions. Because of its specificity and reversibility, nitrosylation affects cellular signaling more selectively than the global redox changes induced by nitric oxide. Nitrosylation regulates kinases through conformational changes or phosphorylation alterations, changes in substrate specificity, or subcellular localization. However, nitrosylation can also chronically activate Ras superfamily GTPases by enhancing guanine dissociation or nucleotide exchange. In murine fibroblasts, RAS nitrosylation activates downstream pathways, including FAK, Src kinase, and MAPK. Despite this, the implications of nitrosylation on the ERK/MAPK pathway and melanoma progression remain unexplored.

MEK inhibition, a widely used antimelanoma strategy, can sensitize melanoma to immune checkpoint inhibitors by enhancing immune cell infiltration and activation though the underlying mechanisms are not yet known. This process correlates with immunogenic cell death (ICD), in which dying cancer cells release damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMP) that act as antigens for dendritic cells (DC) and macrophages when exposed on the membrane or released extracellularly. Key DAMPs include protein kinase R–like endoplasmic reticulum kinase (PERK), calreticulin (CALR), HMGB1, eIF2α phosphorylation, and IL1β release, all of which contribute to the proliferation of CD8+ T cells.

As nitric oxide is immunomodulatory, we investigated the impact of nitrosylation on the ERK-MAPK pathway and ICD in NRAS-mutant melanoma. Inhibiting nitrosylation/NOS, we sensitized the melanoma cells and tumors to targeted MEKi. This sensitization was attributed to sustained ERK dephosphorylation following denitrosylation. NOS inhibition or knockdown enhanced MEKi efficacy, whereas NOS overexpression conferred resistance. Similar results were observed with cysteine-mutated, non-nitrosylable ERK and MEK proteins. In vivo, these findings were corroborated by significant tumor growth restriction and induction/release of ICD DAMPs. Nitrosylation of key DAMPs suggests that inhibiting nitrosylation potentiates MEKi-induced cell death, leading to the release of non-nitrosylated, active DAMPs that trigger ICD. Further mechanistic studies are needed to identify novel vulnerabilities targeting key nitrosylated proteins to combat drug resistance and immune evasion in NRAS-mutant melanomas.
=== METHODS ===
Materials and Methods

Cell culture

Melanoma cell lines WM1366, SW1, and NRAS5; normal melanocytic lines Hermes 2C and 4C; and the HEK293 cells were generously provided by Drs. Keiran Smalley, Kenneth Tsai, and Florian Karreth at Moffitt Cancer Center. Cells with the prefix “YU” are early passage (n < 10) NRAS-mutant melanoma lines isolated from metastasized melanoma tumors of individual patients. The rationale for using these patient-derived cells is their physiologic similarity to human tumors and a low mutational burden besides the melanoma driver mutations (Supplementary Table S1). These were purchased from the Yale Specimen Core at Yale University under a Material Transfer Agreement. As we purchased cultured commercially available cells from Yale University, we did not acquire any patient personal information; thus, no institutional review was needed. The core also provided the following: immortalized Mel-a and Mel-c, which are mouse, pigmented, and isogenic albino melanocytes, respectively; NBMEL 226/227/454, which are primary human skin melanocytes from three individual donors; and primary human skin fibroblasts (NBHF). Detailed mutational profiles of melanoma cells are provided in Supplementary Table S1. Melanoma cell lines were cultured in RPMI 1640 medium, whereas patient-derived melanoma cells were maintained in Opti-MEM (11875-093 and 31985088, Thermo Fisher Scientific), both supplemented with penicillin–streptomycin (15140-122, Life Technologies) and 5% FBS (F-0500D, Atlas Biologicals). For mouse melanocytes, Opti-MEM was supplemented with 7% horse serum (100-508-500, GeminiBio) and 20 nmol/L TPA (524400, Millipore). Primary human melanocytes and Hermes 2C and 4C were cultured in the same medium as that for mouse melanocytes, with the addition of 10 ng/mL basic fibroblast growth factor, 1 ng/mL heparin, and 25 mmol/L IBMX (cat. #F5392, H3149, and 454202, respectively; Millipore). NBHF and HEK293 cells were cultured in high-glucose DMEM (11965092, Thermo Fisher Scientific), supplemented with 10% FBS and penicillin–streptomycin. All cell cultures were treated with a Mycoplasma removal agent (BUF035, Bio-Rad) for at least the first three passages and were regularly tested for Mycoplasma contamination using PCR-based methods (MP0025, Sigma). Most of the “proof-of-principle” experiments were performed using patient-derived cells from more than four individual donors and more than four established melanoma cell lines. Detailed validations were performed using WM1366 (cell line) and YUGASP (patient-derived) melanoma cells due to their faster growth and easier maintenance. For long-term experiments, such as CRISPR knockdowns and overexpression, WM1366 cells were used, as most “YU” cells have limited proliferation.

Inhibition of NOS and MEK

NOS inhibitors (NOSi) included 200 μmol/L 1400 W and 1 mmol/L L-NMMA (S8337 and S7920, Selleckchem), 1 mmol/L L-NAME (0665, Tocris), 1 mmol/L L-NIL, 1 mmol/L L-NIO, 100 µmol/L aminoguanidine, and 1 mmol/L L-NNA (80310, 80320, 81530, 10005031, and 80220, Cayman Chemical). Nitric oxide scavengers included 100 µmol/L carboxy-PTIO (81540, Cayman Chemical). MEKis consisted of 1 to 5 nmol/L trametinib (Tr; 7709, Tocris) and 200 nmol/L selumetinib (AZD6244, S1008, Selleckchem). Cells were pretreated with various NOSi for 24 to 48 hours, followed by MEKi treatment to facilitate the recycling of nitrosylated proteins to their non-nitrosylated forms before MEK inhibition. The two most effective combinations of NOSi were panNOSi-1 (L-NAME + 1400 W) and panNOSi-2 (L-NMMA + 1400 W). After NOS inhibition, cells were treated with the MEKi (Tr) for various time points to assess the expression and phosphorylation status of various proteins and for >72 hours for cell survival assays.

Exogenous overexpression and knockdown of NOS

For orthogonal assessments, NOS2 (iNOS) was exogenously overexpressed using the pLIX403-hNOS2 lentiviral vector (110800, Addgene), which employs a tetracycline-inducible system. NOS2 overexpression was evaluated by Western blotting 24 to 72 hours after doxycycline (S4163, Selleckchem) treatment. For CRISPR-based knockdown, we utilized predesigned and validated lentiviral plasmid constructs from GenScript (sc1805) that included guide RNA 2 (gRNA2; ATC​TAC​AAA​GTC​CGA​CAT​CC) and gRNA3 (AGG​AGG​ACG​CCT​TCC​GCA​GC) targeting iNOS (NOS2), as well as gRNA1 (ACC​GAG​TCT​TCA​ATG​ACC​TA) and gRNA2 (GAC​ATC​ATT​CTT​GCG​GTC​AA) targeting nNOS (NOS1). The gRNAs were incorporated into the pLentiCRISPR version 2 plasmid backbone (SC1818, GenScript). Plasmid transfections were performed using Lipofectamine 3000 (L3000001, Thermo Fisher Scientific). Lentiviral particles were generated in HEK293 cells using psPAX2 and pCMV-VSVG (plasmids #12260 and #8454, respectively; Addgene) and purified according to standard protocols. Following the transduction of lentiviral particles into the WM1366 and YUGASP cell lines, selection was carried out using 0.5 to 1 µg/mL puromycin (A1113803, Thermo Fisher Scientific). Stable knockdown of NOS1 and NOS2 in WM1366 and YUGASP cells was achieved through constant puromycin treatment (>7 days). NOS knockdown was subsequently confirmed by Western blotting.

Cell viability and IC50 assays

Cell viability assays were performed using alamarBlue reagent (DAL1025, Thermo Fisher Scientific) in 96-well plates (3904, Corning) to determine the IC50 values of individual inhibitors, following standard protocols. For combination treatments, IC50 values were assessed using colony formation assays in 12-well plates (CC7682-7512, USA Scientific). Cell growth differences between NOS overexpression and knockdowns, as well as between parental and Tr-resistant (TrR) cells, were also evaluated using colony formation assays. Colonies were stained with 0.1% crystal violet in 1% methanol and 1% formaldehyde for 2 hours. Cell viability was estimated by either counting the colonies directly or by extracting the crystal violet with 10% glacial acetic acid for 2 to 3 hours at room temperature, followed by optical density (OD) measurement at 490 nm. IC50 values and statistical significance were assessed using one- or two-way ANOVA, as well as other appropriate methods in GraphPad Prism.

Kinase array and Western blotting

Cell Signaling Technology: Phospho-ERK (pERK; 9101S), total ERK (9102S), DUSP6 (50945), DUSP4 (5149S), pMEK1/2 (9154), S100B (90393), RhoB (2098), RhoA (2117), RhoC (3430S), Rac1/2/3 (2465T), C-Myc (5605S), ATF2 (35031), pGSK3B (9323S), GSK3B (12456S), RSK-1 (8408S), SPRY2 (14954S), AKT (4691), pAKT (4060), c-Jun (9165), p-c-Jun (3270), GAPDH (2118), α-tubulin (3873), vinculin (13901S), phospho-β-catenin (9561S), β-catenin (2698S), E2F1 (3742S), proliferating cell nuclear antigen (PCNA; 13110), cleaved caspase-3 (9664S/9661S), cleaved caspase-9 (9505), Bcl-xL (2764), cleaved PARP (5625S), Bcl2 (15071S), Mcl-1 (94296), cyclin D1 (12590S), MITF (12590S), and anti-mouse horseradish peroxidase (HRP)–linked (7076S).

Additional sources: Anti-rabbit HRP-linked (4050-05, SouthernBiotech), NOS1 (sc-5302, Santa Cruz Biotechnology), NOS2 (NB300-605, Novus Biologicals), and GBP2 (11854/AP), RASGAP (12935-1-AP), and NRAS (10724-1-AP) from Proteintech.

To identify the pathways affected by sequential inhibition of NOS and MEK, we utilized the Proteome Profiler Human Phospho-Kinase Array Kit (ARY003C, R&D Systems). Patient-derived NRAS-mutant YUGASP cells were treated with 200 µmol/L 1400 W and 1 mmol/L L-NMMA (NOSi) for 48 hours, followed by a combination of NOSi and 2 nmol/L Tr for an additional 24 hours. Approximately 600 µg of cell lysate was used to assess the phosphorylation status of 43 kinases using the kinase array kit, following the manufacturer’s protocol. To further validate and assess the expression and phosphorylation of various kinases and related proteins, standard Western blotting was performed. Briefly, cells were lysed in 1× RIPA buffer (9806S, Cell Signaling Technology) containing a phosphatase–protease inhibitor cocktail, and protein concentration was determined using the Pierce BCA Protein Assay Kit (23225, Thermo Fisher Scientific). The following antibodies were used in the Western blotting experiments:

Flow cytometry

Following respective treatments, the floating cell fraction and adherent cells that were detached using Accutase (423201, BioLegend) were collected and washed with cold PBS. Cells were then stained according to the manufacturer’s protocol (10010-09, SouthernBiotech). Briefly, cells were resuspended in cold 1× Annexin binding buffer, and Annexin V was added. Each tube was gently vortexed and incubated for 15 minutes at 4°C in the dark. After incubation, 7-amino-actinomycin D or DAPI was added directly to the cells. The mixture was immediately analyzed by flow cytometry. Data were analyzed using FlowJo software version 10 and plotted using GraphPad Prism.

Generation of MEKi-resistant cell lines and cell migration assays

TrR cells were generated by gradually increasing the Tr concentration from 2 to 10 nmol/L, followed by chronic Tr treatment >10 passages. The survival of the resistant cells was assessed at various concentrations of MEKi and compared with their MEKi-sensitive counterparts using colony formation assays. Cell migration was also evaluated between Tr-sensitive and TrR cells using a scratch assay, following standard protocols. Briefly, a wide wound or scratch was introduced onto a confluent monolayer of cells in a culture dish. The wound healing, or gap closure due to cell migration, was monitored using time-lapse imaging and analyzed with ImageJ. Data were plotted in GraphPad Prism for further analysis.

Detection of nitrosylated proteins by BST

Nitrosylated proteins were detected using a modified biotin-switch technique (BST; ref.). Cells were lysed directly in HENS (HEPES, EDTA, NaCl, and sucrose) buffer (90106, Thermo Fisher Scientific), supplemented with a protease inhibitor cocktail (78429, Thermo Fisher Scientific). To ensure efficient blocking of free thiols, the pH of the HENS buffer was maintained between 6.0 and 6.5. Free thiols (-SH groups) were blocked with 20 mmol/L N-ethylmaleimide (E1271, Millipore) for 30 minutes at 50°C, and proteins were precipitated with acetone to remove excess N-ethylmaleimide. Nitrosylated (-SNO) thiols were reduced to -SH groups using 1 mmol/L aqueous ascorbate (PHR1279, Sigma) and subsequently labeled with 0.8 mmol/L biotin-HPDP (16459, Cayman Chemical). Excess labeling reagents were removed by acetone precipitation. As a positive control, nitrosylation was induced using chemical donors of nitric oxide, namely S-nitroso-L-glutathione (GSNO; 82240) and diethylenetriamine/DETA-NONOate (DETA; 82120), both from Cayman Chemical. For Western blotting, 10 to 15 µg of biotinylated protein lysate was separated on precast 4% to 20% SDS-PAGE gels (4561091, Bio-Rad), transferred to polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF) membranes (162-0184, Bio-Rad), and detected using either streptavidin–HRP or HRP-tagged anti-biotin antibodies (N100 and 03-3720, Thermo Fisher Scientific). To identify nitrosylated proteins, 600 to 1,000 µg of the biotin-HPDP–labeled protein was diluted with two volumes of neutralization buffer (20 mmol/L HEPES, 100 mmol/L NaCl, 1 mmol/L EDTA, 0.5% v/v Triton X-100). Streptavidin magnetic beads (Z548C, Promega) or streptavidin agarose resin (20359, Thermo Fisher Scientific; 30 µL bead slurry/mg protein) was washed 3 times with 500 µL of neutralization buffer and then added to the biotin-HPDP–labeled protein. Incubation was carried out overnight at 4°C. The beads were washed with neutralization buffer containing 600 mmol/L NaCl, followed by protein elution with elution buffer [neutralization buffer + 5% β-mercaptoethanol (βME)] at 95°C to 100°C for 5 minutes. Eluted fractions were separated by SDS-PAGE and immunoblotted with antibodies of interest to detect the nitrosylation levels of the respective proteins.

Mass spectrometry–based identification of the nitrosylome

Melanoma cells isolated from three individual patients were treated with 100 µmol/L GSNO for 4 hours to induce nitrosylation. The nitrosylome (the nitrosylated fraction of the proteome) was biotin-tagged using BST. Biotinylated proteins were recovered using neutravidin beads (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 29200), followed by trypsin digestion and peptide desalting. Cleaned peptides were labeled with TMT10plex isobaric labeling reagent (90110, Thermo Fisher Scientific) for multiplexing. After label incorporation check (LC/MS-MS and spectral counting of TMT-labeled vs. underivatized peptides), all samples were combined, and another neutravidin enrichment was performed to recover biotinylated peptides. The flow-through peptides were separated with high pH reversed-phase offline fractionation cartridges into four fractions for protein identification. A nanoflow ultra high-performance liquid chromatograph interfaced with an electrospray benchtop Orbitrap mass spectrometer (RSLCnano and Q Exactive HF-X, Thermo Fisher Scientific) was used for LC/MS-MS peptide sequencing experiments. The sample was first loaded onto a precolumn [C18 PepMap100, 100 µm inner diameter (ID) × 2 cm length packed with 5 µm particle size, 100 Å pore size] and washed for 8 minutes with aqueous 2% acetonitrile with 0.1% formic acid. The trapped peptides were eluted onto the analytic column (C18 PepMap100, 75 µm ID × 25 cm length packed with 2 µm particles, 100 Å pore size, Thermo Fisher Scientific). The 120-minute gradient was programmed as follows: 95% solvent A (2% acetonitrile + 0.1% formic acid) for 8 minutes, solvent B (aqueous 90% acetonitrile + 0.1% formic acid) from 5% to 38.5% for 90 minutes, then solvent B from 50% to 90% B for 7 minutes and held at 90% for 5 minutes, followed by solvent B from 90% to 5% in 1 minute and re-equilibration for 10 minutes. The flow rate was 300 nL/minute. Twenty tandem mass spectra were collected in a data-dependent manner following each survey scan. Spray voltage was 1,900 V. Capillary temperature was 275°C. S-lens RF was set to 50. Normalized collision energy was set at 27. The resolution settings were 60,000 and 45,000 for MS and MS-MS, respectively. The isolation window was 0.8 Th with a 0.2 offset to capture the first two isotopes of each peptide for MS-MS. Dynamic exclusion was set at 15 seconds. MaxQuant (version 1.6.14.0; ref.) was used to identify proteins and quantify the TMT reporter ion intensities with default settings: Up to two missed trypsin cleavages were allowed. Carbamidomethyl cysteine was set as a fixed modification. Biotin-HPDP labeling of cysteine and methionine oxidation were set as variable modifications. Both peptide spectral match and protein FDR were set at 0.05. The human protein database was downloaded in March 2021 from Uniprot.org. Related searches were performed in Mascot for data upload to PRIDE/ProteomeXchange (PXD050244).

Site-directed mutagenesis to generate “non-nitrosylable” ERK and MEK mutants

To investigate the function of nitrosylation, we generated “non-nitrosylable” mutants of ERK1 and MEK1 proteins. Potential nitrosylation sites were predicted using the GPS-SNO 1.0 software designed by Xue and colleagues (http://sno.biocuckoo.org/index.php; ref.). The cysteine residues, corresponding peptide sequences, nitrosylation likelihood score (based on an arbitrary cutoff), and the structural clusters of the respective cysteines are summarized in Supplementary Table S2. We obtained the ERK1 and MEK1 expression plasmids from Addgene: pFLAG-CMV-hERK1 (#49328) expressing ERK1/MAPK3 and MEK1-GFP (#14746) expressing MEK1/MAP2K1. Site-directed mutagenesis of selected cysteine into alanine was performed by GeneScript (https://www.genscript.com/mutagenesis.html). The mutation sites are as follows: C178, C183, and C233 for ERK1 and C142, C277, and C341 for MEK1. Mutated plasmids (5–10 µg each) were transfected into HEK293 cells individually using Lipofectamine 3000. The nitrosylation status of the mutants and their wild-type (WT) counterparts was assessed by BST, followed by affinity purification and immunoblotting, as previously described. We also assessed the physiologic impact of the respective mutations on (de)phosphorylation of ERK and its downstream targets in the presence or absence of GSNO and DETA by standard immunoblotting.

 In vivo experiments

We utilized an NRAS-mutant melanoma mouse model developed by Burd and colleagues. This model harbors a codon-specific Q61R mutation in C57BL/6 mouse melanocytes (driven by the Tyr promoter) alongside a concomitant inactivation of p16INK4A. Cells derived from this model, Tyr-CRE-ERT2p16L/LLSL-NrasQ61R/Q61R (TpN61R/61R), referred to as NRAS5 cells, were kindly provided by Dr. Kenneth Tsai at Moffitt Cancer Center. For in vivo tumor formation, we injected 0.5 million cells (in 50 µL) per flank into both flanks of 8-week-old syngeneic C57BL/6 mice (The Jackson Laboratory, Strain #000664) in a 1:1 ratio of medium to Matrigel. This model prompts rapid tumor growth, with tumors typically starting to ulcerate 20 to 22 days after cell injection. Tumor measurements were initiated on days 4 to 5 after injection. Once tumors reached 40 to 50 mm3, mice were treated with NOSi for 48 to 72 hours. This was followed by a combination of NOSi and Tr, starting on days 7 to 8 after injection when the average tumor volume was between 50 and 80 mm3. Treatment continued until days 14 to 16 after MEKi (>22 days after cell injection and >17 days after NOSi treatment initiation) or until either the combination treatment resulted in the lowest tumor volume or the tumors in the vehicle control group began to ulcerate. All treatments were administered via oral gavage. The treatment groups and schedules were as follows: vehicle: 1% DMSO in water; NOSi: 1400 W + L-NNA, daily at 20 mg/kg in water; Tr (MEKi): alternate days at 1 mg/kg in DMSO; and NOSi + MEKi: NOSi daily and Tr every alternate day. To achieve statistical power between 0.8 and 0.9 with a 0.05 error rate, eight mice were used in each treatment group. Tumor size was measured every third day until the end of the experiment. Following sacrifice via CO2 asphyxiation, tumors were excised, measured, fixed in formalin, and paraffin-embedded following standard protocols at Moffitt Cancer Center’s Histopathology Services. Tissue sections (5 µm thick) were then stained for various markers using established protocols. All studies conducted were approved by the University of South Florida’s Institutional Biosafety Committee and the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee in accordance with institutional and federal guidelines.

Hematoxylin and eosin staining and IHC

Paraffin-embedded tissue sections were deparaffinized in xylene and rehydrated through graded ethanol concentrations (100%, 70%, 50%, 10%, and 0% ethanol in water). Antigen retrieval was performed using citrate buffer (pH 6.0; H-3300, VectorLabs) supplemented with 0.05% Tween 20 at 90°C for 15 minutes, followed by incubation under steam pressure at 80°C to 90°C for 30 minutes. Endogenous peroxidases were neutralized with 3% hydrogen peroxide for 15 minutes. After blocking with 10% goat serum (Thermo Fisher Scientific) containing 2% IgG-free BSA (001-000-162, Jackson ImmunoResearch) for 1 to 2 hours at room temperature, slides were incubated overnight at 4°C in a humidified chamber with the primary antibody. Following antibodies were used: PCNA (13110), cleaved caspase-3 (9661S), pERK (4370S), 14-3-3 (pan; 3597), p-eIF2α (70076), and F4/80 (Cell Signaling Technology); PERK (PA540294, Invitrogen); CALR (MAB38981, R&D Systems); HMGB1 (GTX637963, Gentex); IL1β (NBP1-19775SS, Novus Biologicals); and CD11c, CD8, and CD4 (MAB6950SP, MAB116SP, and MAB554SP, respectively, from R&D Systems). Slides were washed 3 times with PBS for 5 minutes each, followed by incubation with a biotinylated secondary antibody (1:1,000; anti-rabbit biotinylated BA-1000, anti-mouse biotinylated BA-9200, VectorLabs) for 1 hour at room temperature. After three additional washes (5 minutes each), positive detection of proteins/antigens was visualized using an ABC reagent and peroxidase substrate DAB (PK-6100 and SK-4100, VectorLabs). The slides were then stained with hematoxylin and eosin using a kit from VectorLabs (H-3502) and mounted with Permount (SP15-100, Thermo Fisher Scientific).

Immune profiling and antigen presentation assay

For immune profiling, single-cell suspensions were prepared from freshly isolated tumor tissue. FACS-based detection of CD8+ and CD4+ T cells, along with cytokines and inflammatory markers, was performed using standard protocols. For the antigen presentation assay, mouse bone marrow–derived DCs (BMDC) were generated as previously described. Briefly, bone marrow precursors were expanded for 6 days with 20 ng/mL GM-CSF in RPMI medium containing 2 mmol/L L-glutamine, 25 mmol/L HEPES, 100 U/mL penicillin–streptomycin, 5 µmol/L βME, and 10% heat-inactivated FBS and maintained at 37°C in a humidified incubator with 5% CO2. On day 6, the BMDC culture medium was supplemented with 20 ng/mL GM-CSF and 0.5 μg/mL lipopolysaccharide; some BMDCs were pulsed with 0.5 μg/mL gp100, as indicated. Additionally, some BMDC media were supplemented with 30% tissue culture supernatants from melanoma cell lines treated with NOSi, Tr, or a combination of both. On day 7, BMDCs were harvested, washed, counted, and plated for coculture and flow cytometry assessment or lysed for qPCR analysis.

BMDC flow cytometry

BMDCs were stained with BioLegend antibodies against CD11c (117335), CD11b (101205), CD80 (104737), CD86 (159216), and CD45 (103128), along with TruStain FcX (101320) and BD Pharmingen antibodies against CD40 (553791) and MHC-I (562363). Viability was assessed using 100 ng/mL DAPI. Samples were analyzed by flow cytometry on a Beckman Coulter CytoFlex II and processed with FlowJo version 11 software. BMDCs were gated on live (DAPI−) CD45+ cells and selected as CD11c+CD11b+.

qRT-PCR

tRNA was isolated from BMDCs using TRIzol (15596026, Invitrogen). Reverse transcription was performed with the Verso cDNA synthesis kit (AB14553B, Thermo Fisher Scientific). qPCR reactions were carried out using SYBR Green (Radiant SYBR Green Master Mix, qPCR #QS1005; Alkali Scientific) on an Applied Biosystems Thermocycler (7900 HT). See Table 1 for primers used.

Mouse Pmel CD8 T-cell isolation

Spleens from Pmel mice (B6.Cg-Thy1a/Cy Tg(TcraTcrb)8Rest/J; RRID: IMSR_JAX:005023) were harvested, and CD8 T cells were negatively enriched using the MagniSort Mouse CD8 T Cell Enrichment Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 8804-6822-74) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. CD8 T cells were stained with 10 µmol/L eBioscience Cell Proliferation Dye eFluor 450 (Invitrogen, 65-0842-85) at a concentration of 4 × 106 cells/mL for 15 minutes in a 37°C water bath, followed by a PBS wash to remove excess dye. Cells were then quenched on ice for 10 minutes. Labeled eF450+ CD8+ T cells were counted and plated in cocultures.

Antigen presentation cocultures

Cocultures were maintained in 200 μL of total media in round-bottom tissue culture–treated 96-well plates. For all cocultures, we used 1 × 105 T cells per well. Following this, 1 × 105 BMDCs per well were added and serially diluted by half to achieve T cell to BMDC ratios ranging from 1:1 to 1:0.125. For controls, Pmel CD8 T cells were cultured alone in the absence or presence of 1 μg/mL gp100. Cocultures were maintained at 37°C in a humidified incubator with 5% CO2 for 72 hours. Cells in coculture were stained with antibodies from BioLegend for CD25 (102024), CD44 (156007), CD69 (104536), CD11c (117309), CD8 (100750), and TruStain FcX (101320) and were assessed by flow cytometry on a Beckman Coulter CytoFlex II. Data were analyzed using FlowJo version 11 software.

Statistical analysis

Each cell culture-based experiment was repeated in more than three distinct cell types, with more than three technical replicates for each. To ensure the robustness of the findings, more than 10 individual donor-derived melanoma cell cultures were utilized. For the in vivo experiments, eight mice per group were used to assess tumor growth with statistical significance. For IHC analyses, >10 images from each tumor in three to five mice per group were evaluated using ImageJ software. Unless mentioned specifically, statistical analyses were performed using one- or two-way ANOVA, depending on the experimental design and other relevant assay formats. GraphPad Prism software was employed to perform these analyses, and results were considered statistically significant when P values were less than 0.05.

Data availability

The mass spectrometry proteomics data for nitrosylomic detection have been deposited in the ProteomeXchange Consortium via the PRIDE partner repository with the dataset identifier PXD050244. All other raw data are available from the corresponding author upon request.
=== RESULTS ===
Results

Inhibition of NOS sensitizes NRAS-mutant melanomas to targeted MEKis

As previously reported, we observed elevated expression of nNOS and iNOS isoforms in melanoma cell lines compared with normal human skin melanocytes (Fig. 1A and B). The allosteric NOSi effectively reduced NOS activity in NRAS-mutant melanoma cells (Fig. 1C; Supplementary Fig. S1A and S1B), without significantly affecting NOS protein expression (Supplementary Fig. S1C). NOS inhibition significantly reduced cell viability after prolonged incubation (>1 week), supporting the role of nitric oxide in melanoma cell survival (Supplementary Fig. S1D).

The hyperactive MEK-MAPK pathway in the NRAS-mutant melanomas promotes cell proliferation and oncogenicity. We used panNOSi-1 and panNOSi-2 combinations (see Materials and Methods) to inhibit all NOS isoforms that sensitized various melanoma cell lines and patient-derived cells to the MEKi, Tr (Fig. 1D–G). NOS inhibition led to a 2- to 100-fold reduction in Tr IC50 values, suggesting that NOS metabolites play a pivotal role in melanoma progression. This growth inhibitory effect was observed in 10 of 13 cell lines. Additionally, patient-derived melanoma cells were sensitized to selumetinib, another MEKi, when combined with NOSi (Supplementary Fig. S1E–S1G). Enhanced apoptosis was observed as a plausible cell death mechanism in response to the combination treatment compared with NOSi or Tr alone, as indicated by Annexin V staining and confirmed by cleaved PARP and activated caspases (Fig. 1H and I; Supplementary Fig. S1H–S1O). However, the detailed underlying mechanisms, as well as validations to determine whether it is apoptosis, necrosis, or senescence, need to be explored.

For in vivo validation, we generated tumors in syngeneic C57BL/6 mice by injecting NRAS5 cells derived from a conditional NRAS knock-in model (TpN61R/61R; see Materials and Methods; ref.). This aggressive model typically forms 40 to 50 mm3 tumors within 4 to 5 days. As expected, 2 to 3 mice in the control group developed large (>400 mm3) and ulcerated tumors by the end of the experiment. However, mice pretreated with NOSi, followed by the NOSi + MEKi combination, showed significant tumor growth inhibition compared with NOS or MEKis alone (Fig. 1J and K). Despite significantly less tumor weight in the combination-treated mice (Fig. 1L), the overall mouse body weight remained unaffected in all groups (Fig. 1M), indicating the treatments were nontoxic. As in vitro, decreased cell proliferation and enhanced apoptosis were observed in tumor tissue sections, indicated by PCNA and caspase-3 staining, respectively (Fig. 1N–P). These findings suggest that NOSi sensitize NRAS-mutant melanomas to MEKis by inhibiting cell growth and inducing apoptosis.

NOS inhibition synergizes with MEKi to abrogate the MEK-ERK signaling cascade

To investigate the mechanisms underlying NOSi-induced sensitivity to MEKi, we examined the phosphorylation of 43 kinases using a kinase array. This revealed differential phosphorylation, primarily dephosphorylation, of several kinases, particularly after sequential treatment with NOSi and MEKi. A summary of kinases involved in the RAS-MEK-ERK cascade is shown in Fig. 2A. The PI3K/AKT pathway, a key player in RAS signaling, was unaffected, whereas the MEK-ERK pathway, a central effector in oncogenic RAS signaling, was downregulated by the combination. Confirming this, we observed prolonged ERK dephosphorylation when NOS was inhibited prior to MEKi treatment in patient-derived NRAS-mutant melanoma cells, including YUGASP, YUDOSO, and YUTICA. This finding was also corroborated in melanoma cell lines such as WM1366, SW1, MelJuSo, and NRAS5 (Fig. 2B–E; Supplementary Fig. S2A–S2J). Although Tr-treated cells gradually regained ERK phosphorylation, NOSi pretreatment maintained its dephosphorylation for over 72 hours (Fig. 2B and C; Supplementary Fig. S2A–S2C).

In addition to ERK phosphorylation, the expression of its downstream oncogenic targets, such as c-Myc, E2F1, c-Jun, and cyclin D1, was further downregulated by the combination treatment (Fig. 2D and E; Supplementary Fig. S2E and S2F). NRAS5 cells, used for the in vivo tumor model, showed similar reductions in pERK and its target proteins (Supplementary Fig. S2G–S2J). Similarly, in vivo in the NRAS-mutant tumors, the combination treatment significantly dephosphorylated ERK (Fig. 2F and G). Downregulated phospho-binding proteins 14-3-3, used as markers for oncogenicity and therapeutic resistance, further emphasized the nitric oxide–mediated (de)regulation of the MEK/ERK signaling and melanoma progression.

As iNOS (NOS2) is often upregulated in melanoma, we stably overexpressed it in WM1366 cells using the pLIX403-hNOS2, a tet-inducible lentiviral plasmid system. This conferred significant Tr resistance (Fig. 2H). Conversely, CRISPR-mediated knockdown of either NOS1 (nNOS, Fig. 2I) or iNOS (NOS2, Fig. 2J) enhanced the antiproliferative effects of MEKi. nNOS or iNOS knockdown also decreased cell viability under basal conditions (Supplementary Fig. S2K and S2L). Doxycycline-induced iNOS expression activated ERK in a dose-dependent manner (Fig. 2K and L), accompanied by increased phosphorylation and expression of downstream targets. The pLIX403 plasmid alone did not induce NOS expression. Additionally, NOS knockdown reduced ERK phosphorylation and downregulated the expression of cell survival proteins in the ERK cascade (Fig. 2M–O). These findings highlight a critical role of NOS in the therapeutic response to targeted MEKis, particularly its impact on MEK-ERK signaling in melanoma.

Nitrosylation regulates multiple signaling pathways in NRAS-mutant melanoma

Nitrosylation is a selective PTM, akin to phosphorylation. Using the BST, we detected nitrosylation in patient-derived cells from various melanoma subtypes (Fig. 3A). Besides driver mutations, these cells exhibited a low mutational burden (Supplementary Table S1), suggesting that passenger mutations have a limited impact on nitrosylation in melanoma. Nitrosylation is labile, often leading to variable immunoblot bands; however, the overall patterns across melanoma subtypes were consistent across replicates. Such experimental variations were further controlled by processing all samples together in BST. Nitrosylation detection was validated using nitrosylated glutathione (GSNO; Fig. 3B and C), which efficiently transnitrosylates thiol groups. As expected, NOSi decreased the nitrosylation (Fig. 3D and E; Supplementary Fig. S3A and S3B), with further reduction observed upon combined MEKi. Tr alone slightly enhanced nitrosylation though not significantly (Fig. 3D and E).

Mass spectrometry profiling of the nitrosylome in three NRAS-mutant melanoma cell lines identified approximately 2,200 nitrosylated proteins, most of which have not yet been reported to be nitrosylated. Using Panther GO analyses (https://www.pantherdb.org/; ref.), these proteins were categorized into various biological processes (Fig. 3F). We highlighted the pathways linked to RAS signaling in Fig. 3G and the nitrosylation levels of proteins involved in RAS-MEK-ERK regulation in Fig. 3H. This screen suggested the nitrosylation of RAS pathway proteins (NRAS, MEK, ERK, Rho GTPases, RSK1, and DUSPs), which may contribute to the targeted therapy response inNRAS-mutant melanomas.

Nitrosylation induces sustained ERK activation in the NRAS-mutant melanomas

We observed enhanced ERK phosphorylation in WM1366 and YUGASP cells when nitrosylation was induced with GSNO, in a dose- and time-dependent manner (Supplementary Fig. S4A–S4D). To assess the sustained effects of nitrosylation on ERK (de)phosphorylation, WM1366 cells were pretreated with GSNO for 4 hours, followed by Tr treatment for 1 to 4 hours. GSNO-induced nitrosylation correlated with ERK phosphorylation and counteracted MEK inhibition (Fig. 4A and B). Alternatively, pretreating WM1366 cells with Tr for 24 hours, followed by GSNO treatment for 1 to 4 hours, rescued ERK from Tr-induced dephosphorylation, resulting in a GSNO-dependent increase in pERK levels (Fig. 4C and D). These findings confirm that nitrosylation is a key regulator of ERK-MAPK signaling, promoting resistance to MEK inhibition. This was further validated by a 24-hour pretreatment with DETA, another nitric oxide donor, which induced nitrosylation and counteracted MEKi effects on ERK dephosphorylation (Fig. 4E and F). Similar results were observed in the patient-derived melanoma line YUGASP (Supplementary Fig. S4E and S4F), in which DETA enhanced pERK levels even in the presence of Tr. Additionally, DETA-induced nitrosylation correlated with increased cell survival in both WM1366 and YUGASP cells (Fig. 4G and H).

For orthogonal validation, exogenous NOS2 (iNOS) overexpression in WM1366 cells (Fig. 2K and L) led to the activation of ERK, even in the presence of Tr (Fig. 4I and J). In contrast, ERK was dephosphorylated when NOS1 and NOS2 were individually knocked down in WM1366 cells using CRISPR (Fig. 2M–O). This effect was reversed when NOS knockdowns were treated with GSNO in a dose-dependent manner (Fig. 4K and L). However, ERK was further dephosphorylated when NOS knockdown cells were treated with Tr (Fig. 4M and N). These results conclude that nitrosylation allows NRAS-mutant melanoma cells to overcome MEK inhibition by sustaining ERK activation.

Nitrosylation induces MEKi resistance in NRAS-mutant melanomas

 NRAS-mutant melanomas often develop resistance against targeted MEKi. To explore the role of nitrosylation in acquired MEKi resistance, we generated TrR WM1366 and SW1 melanoma cells, WM-TrR and SW1-TrR, respectively. These exhibited minimal or no cytotoxicity to 5 to 10 nmol/L Tr, in contrast to their parental counterparts, WM-P and SW1-P, which were sensitive to 1 to 3 nmol/L Tr. Notably, TrR cells displayed enhanced oncogenic properties, including 30% to 50% higher proliferation (Supplementary Fig. S5A) and increased migration in wound-healing assays (Supplementary Fig. S5B and S5C). Although NOSi and Tr alone slowed wound healing partially, sequential NOSi and MEKi treatment reduced cell migration significantly by 3- to 4-fold (Supplementary Fig. S5C), suggesting that NOS plays a critical role in mediating oncogenic traits in NRAS-mutant melanomas. Further, NOS inhibition alone reduced cell viability by 25% to 50% in WM-TrR (Fig. 5A and B) and SW1-TrR cells (Fig. 5C and D). Preincubation with NOSi markedly lowered the IC50 of Tr by ∼30- to 50-fold in WM-TrR cells and ∼40- to 100-fold in SW1-TrR cells. Furthermore, TrR cells demonstrated elevated pERK levels compared with their parental counterparts, and sequential NOSi and MEKi treatment significantly downregulated ERK phosphorylation and the expression of ERK targets (Fig. 5E–G). These findings suggest that nitrosylation-mediated regulation of ERK plays a key role in mediating MEKi resistance and modulating the therapeutic response in NRAS-mutant melanomas.

In parallel, TrR cells exhibited ∼50% higher global nitrosylation than their parental counterparts (Fig. 5H and I). Nitrosylation was significantly reduced in TrR cells when treated with various NOSi and nitric oxide scavengers (Fig. 5H and I). This strongly links nitrosylation-induced ERK activation to acquired MEKi resistance, enhanced cell growth, and increased metastatic potential. To further substantiate this, we compared the viability of parental (Tr-sensitive) and resistant cells in the presence or absence of different NOSi and nitric oxide scavengers. As previously demonstrated (Fig. 1; Supplementary Fig. S1), parental cells showed reduced viability with the combination of NOSi and MEKi. However, this cytotoxic effect was much more pronounced in TrR cells (Fig. 5J). This is clinically relevant because, like patients, TrR cells exhibit enhanced oncogenic potential compared with parental cells. Given that Tr alone did not affect their viability and NOSi enhanced the MEKi-mediated cytotoxicity, it suggests that NRAS-mutant melanomas use nitrosylation to evade MEKi-induced cell death. In conclusion, we demonstrated a direct correlation among nitrosylation, chronic ERK hyperactivation, and resistance to targeted MEK inhibition (MEKi).

Mechanisms underlying nitrosylation inhibition–mediated sensitization of NRAS-mutant melanomas to targeted MEK inhibition

To explore the underlying mechanisms, we induced nitrosylation using GSNO and biotinylated the nitrosylome using BST. As biotin attaches to the -SNO group through a disulfide bond, βME–mediated signal reduction confirmed the detection specificity (Fig. 6A). Coomassie blue staining was used to confirm equal loading for BST (Fig. 6B). When immunodetected, the affinity-purified nitrosylome contained ERK and other MEK-ERK pathway proteins (designated as -SNO in Fig. 6C and D), such as NRAS, Rac, Rho, and ERK-dephosphatases (DUSP4 and DUSP6), along with the proteins that regulate the cellular localization of ERK (RSK1). As biotin is attached to the -SNO group via a disulfide bond in BST, βME–mediated reduction of nitrosylated fractions confirmed their nitrosylation status (Fig. 6C and D). Moreover, total protein levels (inputs) remained unaffected by βME treatment. These results were validated using DETA-mediated nitrosylation induction and DTT as a reducing agent to break disulfide bonds between biotin and nitrosylated cysteines (Supplementary Fig. S6A–S6D).

In parallel, we also detected endogenous nitrosylation of these ERK regulators in the WM1366 cell line and patient-derived YUGASP cells (Fig. 6E–H). Importantly, combining NOS inhibition with Tr reduced the nitrosylation of these regulators, highlighting a synergistic relationship between NOS and the MEK/ERK pathway in promoting melanoma aggressiveness. Although SPRY2 was identified as a potential nitrosylation target, its modification was mainly influenced by MEK inhibition rather than NOS inhibition. Overall, this demonstrated how nitrosylation-mediated regulation of MEK-ERK effectors contributes to sustained ERK hyperactivation.

Non-nitrosylable ERK1 and MEK1 mutants abrogate ERK-MAPK signaling and melanoma cell growth

We identified potentially nitrosylable cysteines of ERK1 and MEK1 proteins using GPS-SNO 1.0 (Materials and Methods) and mutated them into non-nitrosylable alanines (Supplementary Table S2). For ERK1, the C178A and C233A mutants displayed significantly reduced nitrosylation compared with the WT ERK (Fig. 7A–C; Supplementary Fig. S7A and S7B). Physiologically, the C178A and C233A mutants impaired the growth of HEK293 cells (Fig. 7D), whereas WT ERK promoted cell growth. This further correlated with an abrogation of ERK activation upon expression of the C233A and C178A mutants (Fig. 7E and F; Supplementary Fig. S7C and S7D). The GSNO treatment failed to induce nitrosylation and the consequent phosphorylation in these mutants, supporting the idea that C178 and C233 are critical nitrosylation sites (Fig. 7A–C). Moreover, Tr was more potent in dephosphorylating the C233A and C178A mutants compared with WT ERK, reinforcing the importance of these cysteines in ERK activation (Fig. 7E–H).

For MEK, the C142A, C277A, and C341A mutants displayed reduced nitrosylation compared with WT MEK, even in the presence of GSNO, suggesting that all are potential nitrosylation sites (Fig. 7I–K; Supplementary Fig. S7E and S7F). The C142A and C341A mutants significantly inhibited cell growth, whereas the expression of C277A led to hyperproliferation of HEK293 cells (Fig. 7L). Correspondingly, the C142A and C277A mutants caused a marked reduction in ERK phosphorylation compared with WT MEK1, both under basal conditions and in the presence of GSNO (Fig. 7M and N; Supplementary Fig. S7G). Phosphorylation of MEK (pMEK1/2) followed similar trends with the respective MEK mutants (Fig. 7M and N). This was further validated when cells expressing the MEK mutants were treated with MEKi. Although Tr dephosphorylated WT ERK, the expression of the MEK-C341A and MEK-C142A mutants synergized with Tr to completely abolish pERK levels (Fig. 7M and O; Supplementary Fig. S7H). In contrast, overexpression of the MEK-C277A mutant had a minimal impact on ERK phosphorylation. Overall, these findings identify specific cysteine residues (C178 and C233 in ERK1 and C142 and C341 in MEK1) as critical nitrosylation sites that regulate ERK phosphorylation and the resistance mechanisms in NRAS-mutant melanomas.

Nitrosylation regulates antimelanoma immune response in the tumor microenvironment

Nitric oxide modulates antitumor immunity in various cancers, including melanoma. In the TpN61R/61RNras-mutant melanoma model, sequential NOSi and MEKi treatment enhanced the total T-cell population by ∼10% (Fig. 8A). The gating strategy for flow cytometry is detailed in Supplementary Fig. S8A. Although the CD4+ T-cell fraction partially decreased (Fig. 8B; Supplementary Fig. S8B), the combination treatment doubled the CD8+ T-cell population (Fig. 8C and D; Supplementary Fig. S8C and S8D), a clinically significant finding, as enhancing CD8+ T-cell infiltration in melanoma is a major therapeutic challenge.

Our nitrosylomics data identified the nitrosylation of ICD markers, including CALR, HMGB1, PERK, and HSPs (Fig. 8E; ref.). For ICD induction, DAMPs such as CALR and HMGB1 are released extracellularly. We hypothesized that nitrosylation diminishes the immunogenicity of these DAMPs. Validating this, we detected nitrosylated CALR, HMGB1, and PERK in the nitrosylomes purified from GSNO-treated and untreated WM1366 cells (Fig. 8F–I). We then examined whether combination treatment promoted the release of DAMPs into the extracellular space following MEKi-induced cell death. In the TpN61R/61R melanoma model, sequential NOSi and MEKi treatment enhanced CALR and HMGB1 staining in both the cytoplasm and extracellular regions compared with single treatments (Fig. 8J). In addition, the combination treatment significantly induced the extracellular release of other DAMPs, such as phosphorylated eIF2α, IL1β (ICD marker), and the number of tumor-associated macrophages (Fig. 8J). Although further investigation is needed, we hypothesize that macrophages may coordinate ICD via a novel “immune surrender” pathway. ICD is known to activate DCs and engage T-cell responses, and we observed a significant increase in CD11c signal with the NOSi + MEKi combination, indicating enhanced DC frequency or infiltration (Fig. 8J, last panel). These results suggest that NOSi + MEKi treatment promotes ICD and immune activation in NRAS-mutant melanomas.

Supporting this, we demonstrated the extracellular release of HMGB1, CALR, and PERK into the conditioned medium of human and mouse melanoma cells, with an exclusive and significant elevation in the combination-treated groups (Fig. 8K and L). This was validated by quantitating the cellular and extracellular release of HMGB1 and CALR in the immunostained sections from Fig. 8J (Supplementary Fig. S8E). In an antigen presentation assay, BMDCs treated with conditioned medium from NOSi + MEKi–treated melanoma cells showed increased expression of costimulatory markers (CD40 and CD86), whereas the frequency of mouse BMDCs remained unchanged (Fig. 8M and N). The generation and expansion of BMDCs are demonstrated in Supplementary Fig. S8F. This was accompanied by elevated mRNA expression of pattern recognition receptors (Tlr2, Tlr4, and Cd91) in BMDCs, induced by HMGB1 and CALR present in the conditioned medium from NOSi + MEKi–treated melanoma cells (Fig. 8O; Supplementary Fig. S8G). These findings suggest that the NOSi + MEKi combination specifically activated BMDCs compared with the single treatments. Coculturing the naive Pmel CD8+ T cells with various ratios of the previously activated BMDCs pulsed with gp100 (CD8+ T cells: BMDCs = 1:0.5–1:0.125) increased the Pmel CD8+ T-cell proliferation compared with controls (Fig. 8P and Q; Supplementary Fig. S8H–S8J). This was accompanied by upregulated activation markers (CD69, CD25, and CD44) on CD8+ T cells (Fig. 8Q). These results confirm the activation of DCs by the denitrosylated DAMPs released from NOSi + MEKi–treated melanoma cells that, in turn, stimulated tumor-specific CD8+ T-cell activation and proliferation. The underlying molecular mechanisms are still under investigation.

In conclusion, we showed that nitrosylation induces MEKi resistance by upregulating the ERK-MAPK signaling in melanoma. Accordingly, nitrosylation inhibition–mediated MEKi sensitization releases immunogenic DAMPs that induce ICD. The synergistic effects of NOS and MEK inhibition, including ICD activation, suggest a positive feedback loop between NOS and MEK/ERK, driving oncogenicity and MEKi resistance in NRAS-mutant melanoma.
=== DISCUSS ===
Discussion

Oncogenic RAS mutations induce NOS activity. Although nitric oxide is short-lived and pleiotropic, it primarily regulates cell signaling through nitrosylation, a reversible PTM that affects protein activity, stability, and localization. Nitration, another NOS-induced PTM, competes with tyrosine phosphorylation and is often inhibitory. Based on this premise and our findings that NOS inhibition synergized with MEKis (Figs. 1 and 2), we hypothesized that nitrosylation constitutively activates MEK-ERK signaling in NRAS-mutant melanoma. This was substantiated further by the minimal effect of exogenous NOS2 overexpression on MEK phosphorylation (Fig. 2K and L), suggesting that the underlying mechanisms are specific and likely involve nitrosylation rather than the global redox effects of nitric oxide. Although BRAF-mutant and WT BRAF/NRAS melanomas exhibited comparable nitrosylation (Fig. 3), we primarily focused on the NRAS-mutant subtype due to its aggressiveness and lack of effective therapies.

Despite known denitrosylases such as thioredoxin and S-nitroso glutathione reductase that can globally denitrosylate nitrosylated proteins, protein-specific denitrosylation has not been identified so far. Accordingly, we first correlated nitrosylation modulation with MEKi sensitization in NRAS-mutant melanoma cells (Figs. 1–3). The average half-life of mammalian proteins is 0.5 to 35 hours. Thus, a 24- to 48-hour NOSi pretreatment allowed nitrosylated proteins to be recycled with their non-nitrosylated versions before MEKi treatment. NOSi alone had minimal effect on melanoma cell survival unless the treatment was prolonged (Figs. 1–4; Supplementary Figs. S1 and S2). This, combined with significant modulation of nitrosylation by NOSi (Fig. 3; Supplementary Fig. S3), further supports the role of nitrosylation over nonspecific redox stress induced by nitric oxide in regulating melanoma growth. NRAS-mutant melanomas often develop resistance to targeted MEKi. Elevated global nitrosylation in MEKi-resistant cells, coupled with marked sensitization to MEKi following denitrosylation, indicates that nitrosylation contributes to resistance (Fig. 5; Supplementary Fig. S5). Although mutations acquired by melanoma cells could represent an alternate resistance mechanism, our findings from individual donor melanoma cells, which contained limited mutations beyond the pathologic NRAS (Supplementary Table S1), eliminate this possibility.

Nitrosylation is influenced by several factors, including protein stability, folding, tertiary structures, and the expression rate of new proteins for recycling with non-nitrosylated versions. Further, as NOSi does not completely inhibit NOS, compensatory activity from NOS isoforms may sustain nitrosylation on certain proteins (Fig. 6). To address these discrepancies, we profiled the nitrosylome (Fig. 3) using nitrosyl donors such as GSNO and DETA, a widely used strategy that accounts for the highly labile and variable nature of nitrosylation levels in cultured cells. It also helps distinguish true nitrosylation events from reduced protein disulfide bonds, S-glutathionylation, and ambiguities in site assignment. Thus, several known and potentially novel nitrosylated proteins were revealed in NRAS-mutant melanomas, including ERK, MEK, NRAS, DUSPs, and RSK1 (Figs. 3 and 6; Supplementary Fig. S6). Although all these proteins are potentially critical effectors in NRAS-mutant melanoma and will be pursued in future studies, we focused on ERK and MEK, which are central regulators of the RAS-MEK-ERK pathway. Denitrosylation of selected sites sensitized melanoma cells to MEKi-mediated downregulation of the ERK-MAPK pathway (Fig. 7). For ERK, we identified C178 and C233 as primary nitrosylation sites, which contrasts with the previously identified C183. However, we utilized various chemical sources and orthogonal approaches to validate C178 and C233, in several cell types, compared with a limited nitric oxide source used on nonmelanoma cells previously. The mechanisms underlying MEK and ERK nitrosylation and their role in hyperactivating the ERK-MAPK pathway are currently under investigation.

Targeted MEKi combined with immunotherapy is often utilized to treat melanoma. About this, we observed restricted tumor growth, release of DAMPs, and ICD induction, with a concomitant enhancement of the CD8+ T-cell repertoire in vivo when NOS is inhibited prior to MEKi (Fig. 8; Supplementary Fig. S8). This, validated further by the detection of nitrosylated DAMPs and DCs: T-cell cocultures strategy, suggested nitrosylation inhibition as a promising strategy for counteracting immune evasion in melanoma. Moreover, NOS inhibition also induced macrophage infiltration, which may facilitate tumor cell phagocytosis and bolster the antimelanoma immune responses. The enhanced macrophage presence in response to the combination treatment is particularly noteworthy. Macrophages play a critical role in the immune response by mediating the phagocytosis of cancer cells, aiding cytotoxic tumor killing, and supporting both innate and adaptive immunity. Notably, recent studies have shown that although DCs phagocytose dead tumor cells to induce long-term adaptive immunity via ICD, macrophages can sense uncontrolled tumor proliferation and mediate “immune surrender” by phagocytosing live tumor cells through CXCL12/CD47/CXCR4 signaling modulation. This and previous studies suggest that although ICD and immune surrender are independent processes, their interplay might be regulated by specific molecular pathways. Though the underlying mechanisms are still under investigation, we believe that although nitrosylation inhibition induces ICD upon MEKi treatment, nitrosylation also triggers the internalization of CD47 by regulating its interaction with CXCR4. In conclusion, we demonstrated that sequential NOS and MEKi activated DCs and CD8+ T cells, contributing to antimelanoma immunity (Fig. 8).

Mechanistically, we validated the extracellular release of DAMPs into the conditioned medium of the melanoma cells treated with NOSi and MEKi. This conditioned medium activated cultured DCs, which in turn proliferated and activated CD8+ T cells in a DC:CD8+ T-cell coculture (Fig. 8), clearly demonstrating the role of nitrosylation in regulating antimelanoma immune memory. However, despite its evident role in regulating MEK-ERK and ICD, the source and quantity of nitric oxide produced within the tumor microenvironment remain to be fully investigated. Nonmelanoma cells, such as macrophages and myeloid-derived suppressor cells, also produce nitric oxide, complicating the role of melanoma cell–specific NOS activity. Based on our global NOS inhibition in vivo, we believe that regardless of the source, nitric oxide dominantly promotes melanoma progression. Furthermore, although nitrosylation is known to both promote and inhibit melanoma progression, our in vivo model, along with various melanoma cell lines and patient-derived cells, consistently showed that nitrosylation inhibition correlates with reduced melanoma proliferation and immune evasion.

Conclusions

We conclude that oncogenic NRAS upregulates NOS activity, driving nitrosylation-mediated hyperactivation of the MEK-ERK pathway. Nitrosylation also impairs the immunogenicity of intrinsic melanoma DAMPs, which, together with MEK-ERK hyperactivation, promote tumor progression and immune evasion. A detailed investigation of the intrinsic factors will reveal potentially novel therapeutic targets for NRAS-mutant melanoma.
